---
title: "Carbonate and gas chemistry"
---

Why can two waters with the same pH respond differently to an acid input?
Carbonate equilibria connect dissolved carbon, acid neutralisation, gas exchange,
and mineral stability. We will use a deliberately simple freshwater model to
separate these effects.

Start with [carbonate species and alkalinity](lec.qmd), then
[gas exchange and minerals](gases-lec.qmd). Work through the
[exercises](exercise.qmd), including a short R activity. The
[model and reference sheet](reference.qmd) supplies all constants and assumptions.
The reading context is chapters 10–11 of vanLoon and Duffy, fourth edition;
precise subsection assignments remain to be selected.

## What you should be able to do

- Calculate carbonate species ratios at a supplied pH and interpret a distribution diagram.
- Distinguish pH, total dissolved inorganic carbon, alkalinity, and buffer capacity.
- Explain why a strong-acid input and carbon dioxide uptake change water differently.
- Apply a specified Henry coefficient and a simple calcite saturation test.
- Use a supplied R calculation to plot species fractions, check it against a hand
  calculation, and explain what the plot cannot predict.

## Before starting

You need concentration units, an equilibrium expression, logarithms, and a
balanced acid–base reaction. Recall that one millimole per litre is
$10^{-3}$ mol/L, and one micromole per litre is $10^{-6}$ mol/L.
Under our dilute-solution approximation,
$\mathrm{pH}=-\log_{10}[\mathrm{H^+}]$ when the numerical concentration is in
mol/L. Thus pH 7 corresponds to $10^{-7}$ mol/L, and lowering pH by one means
ten times more hydrogen ion. The exact pH definition uses activity.

Try before reading further: does pH 8 tell you how many moles of acid a litre
of water can neutralise? What additional information might you need?

## A catchment connection

Acid deposition can change the acid input to a lake. Catchment minerals,
soil exchange, organic acids, and biological activity also influence the water.
Here we isolate carbonate chemistry first. All numerical waters are constructed
teaching examples, not measurements from a real lake. The gas-exchange examples
are separate boundary conditions, not an assumed continuation of the closed-water
acid experiment.
